blocks.text: Design a movie ticket booking system, the mechanism behind selecting one or more specific seats for a given showtime, holding them briefly while payment completes, and permanently booking them on success. This is the final problem in this category, and it introduces a genuinely different shape of inventory than every prior design here. Flash sale managed a single undifferentiated scalar count of one item. Amazon managed a per-product quantity across multiple warehouses. This is a fixed GRID of individually identified seats, and a single customer request can name several specific seats at once that must be reserved together, as one atomic, all-or-nothing group.

blocks.alt: A customer selecting several specific seats triggers a multi-seat atomic lock: every seat free means all are held together, even one seat already taken means the entire request is rejected with none held

blocks.text: The two techniques that define this design are multi-seat atomic locking, where a request naming several specific seats either succeeds entirely or fails entirely with none reserved, and a time-limited hold that automatically releases back to available if payment is not completed before its own timer runs out, but converts to a permanent booking, no longer subject to any timer, the instant payment succeeds.

blocks.text: A customer should be able to view a showtime's current seat map, seeing which seats are available, held by someone else, or already booked. A customer should be able to request several specific seats together, with the request succeeding only if every one of those seats is currently available. A held group of seats should automatically release back to available if the customer does not complete payment within a bounded time window. Completing payment should convert a held group into a permanent booking that no longer expires. Every viewer of a showtime's seat map should see availability changes reflected in close to real time.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter here, and the first two are what most define this problem's core difficulty.

blocks.alt: No two customers ever booked the same seat, a multi-seat selection never partially reserved, real-time seat map updates for every viewer, automatic release of an abandoned hold, and a fast selection experience

blocks.text: No two customers ever being booked the same seat is the single most important guarantee, a double-booked seat is a real, visible, embarrassing failure the moment two people arrive at the theater. A multi-seat selection never being partially reserved means a customer choosing three seats together should never end up owning only two of them, that would be a strictly worse outcome than an honest, upfront rejection. Real-time seat map updates mean another shopper looking at the same showtime should see a seat turn unavailable within roughly a second of someone else holding it. Automatic release of an abandoned hold means a customer who selects seats and then simply closes the browser should not permanently deny those seats to everyone else. And a fast selection experience means checking an entire group of requested seats needs to complete in a small fraction of a second.

blocks.text: This design assumes a fixed, platform-wide hold duration for simplicity, though the same underlying mechanism supports per-theater configuration equally well. Payment processing is assumed to reuse the payment system this project already covers, triggered only once a hold is confirmed by the customer. Modifying an active hold is assumed to require releasing it and submitting a new request for the full desired group, keeping the atomic all-or-nothing guarantee simple rather than layering incremental modification logic on top of it.

blocks.text: A single extremely popular showtime can realistically have hundreds of shoppers viewing and attempting to select seats from its map at once, especially in the moments right after tickets go on sale. Each individual theater's seat map is a fixed, modestly sized grid, rarely more than a few hundred seats, which keeps any single multi-seat lock check small and fast regardless of how many shoppers are competing for it. That check needs to complete in well under a second to keep seat selection itself feeling instant.

blocks.text: A customer's requested group of seats reaches the seat selection service, which hands it to the multi-seat lock manager to evaluate against that showtime's single authoritative seat map. If every requested seat is currently available, all of them are held together; if even one is not, the entire request fails with none held. The hold expiry scheduler independently tracks each active hold's own timer, releasing seats automatically if payment is not completed in time, while a completed payment converts a hold into a permanent booking through the payment service.

blocks.text: A held group of seats exists in a bounded, temporary state tied to one customer. If that customer completes payment before the hold's own timer runs out, the seats convert to a permanent booking that no longer expires under any circumstance. If the timer runs out first, the seats are automatically released back to available for any other shopper to select.

blocks.text: Each seat's current status is modeled as a single, fast, in-memory-backed value per showtime rather than being derived from a scan of booking history on every request, since a multi-seat check needs to complete in well under a second even for a large group. Every hold and its eventual outcome, confirmed or expired, is still durably recorded, useful both for customer support and for detecting scalping patterns after the fact.

blocks.text: The happy path is the atomic hold flow above, a group of seats cleanly checked and held together. The workflow worth walking through separately is the partial-conflict case, where a customer requests a mix of available and unavailable seats: rather than silently granting only the available subset, which would surprise the customer with fewer seats than they chose, the entire request is rejected, and the customer sees an honest, accurate seat map to make a new selection from.

blocks.text: This mirrors the structural, single-writer-per-resource pattern this project has already used for flash sale's single stock counter and the online auction's single item state, applied here per showtime, one showtime's seat map cannot be split across multiple writers without risking a double-booked seat, but because each of many different showtimes owns its own independent writer, the system as a whole still scales horizontally.

blocks.text: Scalping and denial-of-seating abuse, a single actor repeatedly holding large blocks of seats purely to deny them to genuine shoppers or resell them, is this design's defining security concern, distinct from every other category's angle in this project, since the hold mechanism that makes checkout convenient is exactly the mechanism such abuse would exploit.

blocks.text: A showtime's single authoritative writer latency is the most important thing to watch, since every seat request for that showtime depends on it directly with no parallel fallback by design. The rate of holds that expire without ever converting to a booking is also worth tracking, an unusually high abandonment rate on one showtime can signal either a confusing checkout flow or genuine scalping activity worth investigating.

blocks.text: A change to the multi-seat lock manager's own all-or-nothing logic needs the most rigorous possible testing in this system, since any bug there risks either a double-booked seat or a customer being wrongly denied a genuinely available selection, both real, high-visibility failures for a business built on a physical, in-person experience. Hold duration deserves careful tuning against real checkout completion data, a duration too short frustrates genuine customers mid-payment, while one set too long lets seats sit needlessly unavailable for other shoppers.
